articles.title: Welcome to November’s edition
articles.author: Shepley Magazine Team
articles.summary: From the Domesday Book to the planning boom: what new housing could mean for Shepley, a name for the Cask and Spindle, and bonfire night.
body: We know that Shepley is an ancient settlement, described in the Domesday Book in 1086 as “waste” after the Harrying of the North in 1069/70. However, less than two hundred years later in 1217, Shepley seems to have recovered with the names of local landowners appearing in feudal records. Shepley then progressed through the Middle Ages with agriculture being the primary source of work and later the weaving of cloth and tailoring. In the Victorian era the village woke to the industrial revolution, with the railway arriving in 1850 and Shepley boomed.

The Victorian and Edwardian periods were a time of great development in the village. Many of the fine stone houses and pubs that we see today were built at that time. There was some construction in the late sixties and early seventies but nothing particularly large scale until now when planning applications for new developments have soared, not just in Shepley but throughout our local region. We are now talking about several hundred proposed new properties throughout our area. Shepley and the other villages concerned will be changed forever with increased pressure on our roads and local services. New houses are needed, but is the destruction of ancient green land a positive or a negative thing? Please let us have your comments to our letters page.

Our local pubs very much represent the earlier times with their sturdy stone construction and names depicting Shepley’s agricultural past and industry. What could be better in a village like ours than traditional pub names like The Farmers Boy, The Black Bull and even The Sovereign which represents the founding of Seth Senior’s famous village brewery. The one village pub which could do with a new name is The Cask and Spindle (previously The Railway Hotel). Although it’s been closed for seven years, the brewery has recently received planning consent for exterior lighting so a renaissance might be on the cards. Let’s hope a new village appropriate name goes with it. How about The Shepley Lion as the famed but mysterious beast was first reported to the police in a phone call from this pub where it had reportedly been seen in the car park, (could it have been a Jaguar) in 2011? Anyway, it kept the police busy for a few hours and train passengers were not allowed to leave the luxury of their carriages parked at the station where it had also been spotted (no it wasn’t a Leopard either). So, there’s a unique piece of Shepley history waiting to be immortalised.

That elusive creature was reported the day after bonfire night in 2011, which brings us to our village’s favourite annual event at the cricket field on November the 5th as usual. Brian has been busy for weeks now building the giant structure and he and the whole cricket club team deserve our thanks for putting on this fantastic event every year. There is one important request here, please leave your car at home if you possibly can. If you walk to the event, you will have a far easier time and won’t have to worry about receiving a ticket from the police. On this night of all nights, it’s important that emergency service vehicles can safely navigate the road. There’s an article in this month’s issue from the cricket club with full information on this spectacular event.

articles.title: Shepley Women’s Institute: Our clubs continue to keep busy
articles.author: Shepley WI
articles.summary: Fair Trade tea and coffee talk, the Strollers at Farnley Tyas, Gardening Group at the Health Centre and Crafts and Crumbs.
body: At a recent members’ meeting we had a fascinating presentation by our very own ‘Man from Del Monte’, tea and coffee buyer Paul Jefferies, who taught us about processes to encourage sustainable tea and coffee farming and how Fair Trade organisations work to support young, female farmers across the globe.

Our clubs have been busy as usual. The Strollers enjoyed a gentle, though slightly wet walk around the lanes at Farnley Tyas, finishing with what was intended to be a light lunch at The Golden Cock, though I have it on good authority that several portions of sticky toffee pudding were consumed!

The Gardening Group cut back the hedging shrubs at the entrance to Shepley Health Centre to allow better visibility for drivers exiting the car park. They hope to return in spring to give the Cornus shrubs a good prune to encourage more red stems next autumn. Crafts and Crumbs members are busy working on a variety of personal projects, including embroidered pictures and cushions, knitted Christmas baubles and crochet throws, to name a few. It’s great that we have such a range of skills in this group as there is always someone on hand to help pick up dropped stitches, sort out tangled threads and occasionally unstick glued together fingers!

Our next members’ meeting is scheduled for 2.00pm on Wednesday 18th November, when we hope to enjoy a practical Christmas crafts activity. However, we are unable to confirm at this point that the meeting will go ahead, as, at the time of writing, we do not have an incoming committee to take over following our AGM. As explained in the October article, most of us have already ‘served our time’ on the committee (some doing several stints over the years!) and many members have other commitments which prevent them from stepping up. As the timing of our AGM is after the 12th October deadline date for submission of this article, the result of the voting will not be published until December, but, whatever the outcome, we will keep you informed!

articles.title: Shepley Naturalists’ Society: The year turns
articles.author: Graham Bennett & Rodger Schofield
articles.summary: A stroll around Wentworth Castle and the first winter walk at Dale Dyke Reservoir.
body: ## Wentworth Castle stroll

For the last outing of the summer season, a group of eight tackled the grounds of Wentworth Castle, in sunny if slightly blustery weather. Considering recent rainfall, the ground was firm, but the lack of water in the admittedly small lake was significant. No ducks or geese for once.

Deer were spotted lazing under trees, but all without antlers. Perhaps the males were away on a stag do somewhere. There was a good display of autumn crocus (colchicum cilicicum), while many trees were hanging on well beyond their normal lifespan.

Lunch was taken in the formal garden, followed by a visit to Stainborough Castle at the top of the site. Four intrepid members took the stairs to the top of the tower and enjoyed the views of the surrounding countryside. The restored conservatory was next, followed by ice cream at the cafe, rounding off a pleasant ramble.
— Graham Bennett
## Dale Dyke Reservoir – the first of our monthly winter walks

On a lovely sunny day in early October, we drove over to Dale Dyke reservoir situated off the Strines Road. Our walk started down the zigzag path below the dam embankment, passing the information board reminding us that this was the dam that collapsed causing a disastrous flood in Sheffield.

Today this area is heavily wooded, and the path around the side of the reservoir has lots of tree roots needing a bit of care to walk on it. A few birds were calling, mostly robins, while a scattering of mallards were on the low reservoir foraging on the mud banks. As it is the start of autumn various varieties of fungi were to be seen, fly agaric with its red top and a number of blushing wood mushrooms.

After walking up to the head of the reservoir we stopped for a sandwich overlooking the higher Strines Reservoir next to the very isolated cottage there. In the last few years, the cottage has been refurbished and is now lived in. Our path then followed the upper track where we watched a couple of buzzards soaring overhead, passed another house and then continued beneath a large well-maintained manor house. A diversion of the track near a farm took us past inquisitive goats, back to the road and thence to the car.
— Rodger Schofield

articles.title: Shepley Methodist Church: Is something missing?
articles.author: Kimm
articles.summary: Friendship and belonging, the Oasis café, November preaching rota and Harvest raising over £500 for WaterAid.
body: A recent survey found that 5% of young people aged 16-21 have no close friends, up from 1% in 2014. A news article says that phubbing, (short for snubbing people by focussing on your phone) is destroying relationships. You can see this in people glued to their phones and oblivious to the world around them. Today’s “me, me, me” culture, where we’re led to believe that life is all about what “I” want or need, doesn’t help either. People seem to be losing the confidence and ability to form relationships. It’s no wonder mental health problems are increasing.

It’s also not surprising that there’s a revival in Christian faith growing in this country and around the world. You see it in celebrities and sports people publicly praising God and in growing numbers of church attenders in our towns and cities (it takes a while for new trends to make it into the more rural areas, like Shepley). People are finding friendships, feeling valued and a sense of belonging in meeting with other Christians. Learning to look outwards, to care for others, brings unexpected joy.

If you’re wondering if there’s something that you’re missing in life, you’re welcome to pop into our Oasis cafe on Monday or Friday afternoons, 1:30-3:30. Feel free to bring along some knitting, craft or puzzles to share or just yourself. You’re always welcome to join our services on Sunday mornings from 10:45-11:45 or our monthly Bible studies on the last Sunday of the month from 9:30-10:30. If you think there’s something else we could offer our community, please let us know. The congregation at this year's Harvest were challenged as to how they might use their (symbolic)12 baskets of crumbs, hearing those were left over after Jesus had miraculously made sure some 5,000 + people had enough to eat, despite only five loaves and two fish being offered.

articles.title: St Paul’s Church: Remembering
articles.author: Rev Lindsey Barber
articles.summary: November, the season of remembering – a hand-made poppy, All Souls, and the services for November.
body: November is the season of remembering. I always feel blessed to have the gift of memory when so many other people have limited or no memories, caused by either trauma or illness. We are blessed to be able to recall memories that bring us joy. Remember the days when we used to play outside as children; when we rode on our bikes and built dens. Remember when we got a new job, moved into our own place, maybe got married and had children. Remember the 50’s, 60’s, 70,’s 80’s, 90’s? maybe longer or more recent; the friends you’ve made, the jobs you’ve had, the cars you’ve driven; everything and everybody you have loved.

Armistice Day falls within the Church’s season of remembering, after the festivals of All Saints (1st November) and All Souls (2nd November), during which we remember those whom we love but see no longer.

Maybe you wear a poppy on and around Armistice Day. This is a deeply personal and individual sentiment. About five years ago my daughter gifted me with a beautiful, hand-made poppy. The lady who made them, made an individual poppy for each of the British service personnel who lost their lives during the Afghan War. My poppy is number; 167 of 454. I wear my poppy to remember Private Robert McLaren of The Black Watch, 3rd Battalion, The Royal Regiment of Scotland (3 Scots), who died in Sangin Helmand Province aged 20years on 12th June 2009. Although I never met Robert McLaren, he plays a large part in my life; I am somehow connected to him through the poppy I wear.
Maybe you visited our Heritage Weekend in September and read about some of the people of Shepley who lived, worked and died here.

The people of Israel in the Bible were good at remembering. They told and retold stories of their ancestors who had played an important role in their history. Both you and I do the same thing. We tell and re-tell the stories of those who have gone before us as a way of remembering. During this season of remembering, before we jump ahead to Christmas, let’s bring to mind all those whom we love but see no longer.

articles.title: Hear from our advertisers: Zumba with Tricia
articles.author: Tricia
articles.summary: Former Shepley Band conductor Tricia brings feel-good dance fitness to St Paul’s Church Hall on Thursday mornings.
body: I'm Tricia and I moved to Huddersfield in the summer of 2015 with my partner. I'm a jobbing musician and I conducted Shepley Band for many years, until very recently. I'm currently branching out into other areas.

Two years ago I was far too fat and unhealthy, so much so that my GP referred me to a lifestyle / diet coach. As part of the deal, I was allowed access to the local leisure centre in Huddersfield for a free “try before you buy” fitness month. There was so much variety and I attended many different types of class and activity, finding the dance fitness most appealing. Zumba, in particular, was especially invigorating and satisfying. I still maintain my KAL membership and attend as many classes as I'm able.

The experience was an utter revelation. Gradually, class by class, dance by dance, I got more energetic, fitter and thinner. I've found a fresh energy to life and it's fantastic. I'm hoping to bring this, accompanied by some infectious music, to the good people of Shepley.

What I've started in Shepley is a chance to share some feel- good dance vibes. I was a bit nervous in my first class but, week by week, I'm gradually feeling much more at home. The church hall next to St Paul's, is central and accessible, a wonderful ideal space for this kind of activity.
Soon, if enough folk are interested, I'm going to introduce chair-based Zumba and perhaps Chi Chi Fit, a dance exercise class based on Broadway-style routines and memorable show tunes.
Why not come and join me on Thursday morning and show us all your moves? As strenuous or relaxed as you prefer to make it - it's better when you're dancing :-)

articles.title: Reflections on… My time as an Evacuee in Shepley (Part 1)
articles.author: Angela Sexton (née Stiff)
articles.summary: Sent from London to Smithy Hill in 1942: life with Mr and Mrs Dransfield, the fields off Jos Lane and wartime school dinners.
body: I was born in Fulham in 1938. I had two older brothers, John aged 13 and Graham aged 10. We were living in Pimlico and my brothers were attending Battersea Grammar School. Soon after war broke out my father was sent on active service in Palestine and later transferred to the Indian Army. On the 1st of September 1939 the boys were evacuated, with their school, to Worthing in Sussex. They attended school on half days as they shared the buildings with Worthing High School for Boys. To be near the boys, mother moved down to Sussex with me, and this is where my sister was born.

In the middle of 1940, due to the Battle of Britain, Battersea Grammar School was re- evacuated to Hertford and mother returned to Croydon where she could look after my grandmother and great aunt. She decided, for my safety, to arrange a private evacuation in the country. So it was, that in February 1942 I moved to Smithy Hill Shepley to live with Mr and Mrs Dransfield.

Mr Dransfield had been deafened in World War One trenches and worked as a night foreman in the woollen mill at the bottom of Stretchgates opposite Far Bank, Shelley. Mrs Dransfield was the homemaker, a fantastic cook, superb needlewoman and extremely house proud. Mrs Dransfield made all my clothes from recycled material.

There was only one room upstairs and I slept in a small bed in the corner. I was not allowed upstairs except to go to bed. Mr Dransfield slept during the day and as the cottage was so small I was sent out to play with the other children in the village. I came back for my dinner and then for my tea - two trips down the “flags” and two trips back! The path was spotless and had to remain so!

I spent a great deal of time in the fields off Jos Lane, picking wildflowers and blackberries in the autumn. I went down Stone Wood Lane to the stream where I ‘fished’ for tiddlers. Harvest time was great. Mr Dransfield would put me out of the window at the back of the cottage, with a big stick. As the tractor went round the field cutting the corn the rats would come out. I would chase them with my stick.

The Rec was a great place as it had a seesaw and swings and up the hill was the reservoir. When it was wet, I would go to the farm opposite Smithy Hill and play in their barn. There were steps up to a loft where there was a wooden 3-seater loo!

I have fond memories of attending the local school. The central hall seemed enormous, it was where we had our dinner at big trestle tables. These were long, with possibly 12 children on each side, the teacher one end and an older pupil the other. A pile of plates was placed by the teacher. Dinner would arrive in big metal containers, served out and passed down the table. It was wartime so we were expected to eat everything. My favourite was rice pudding and if you had been good, you were given the container to scrape out. Wonderful! On my final day, before returning to London I scraped out the rice pudding container.

We used trays of sand in which to practise forming our letters and digits, much as whiteboards are used in schools today. Once mastered we progressed to paper and pencil. There was a big clock in the small hall, and I learnt to tell the time at a very early age. The teacher would send a child out to find out the time and if you returned with the correct answer, you were allowed home 5 minutes early. I remember loving to hear the teacher reading stories and she also read poetry to us. In April 1945 I learnt William Wordsworth’s poem ‘I wandered lonely as a cloud’. Mr and Mrs Dransfield didn't read to me, but when I returned to Croydon after the war my mother did and she loved poetry too so we would recite Wordsworth’s poem together.
Each year Mrs Dransfield would have a professional photo of me taken to send to my mother.

We entered the school by separate doors and our coats hung in rows along the wall. There were no toilets inside, they were in a brick outhouse in the playground. The urinals were open to the skies, surrounded by a brick wall whereas the girls were in a covered outhouse. Needless to say, you kept well away from the urinals.

The school is up a steepish hill and there was a very big brick wall by the playground. If you looked over this to the field below you could watch the goats. There was a cottage on Lane Head Road, opposite Firth Street where a lady sold sweets from her front room and I remember buying liquorice sticks from her. On one occasion the cockerel she kept with her chickens attacked me, which made me very wary of chickens. Angela Sexton (nee Stiff) To be continued

articles.title: Friends of Shepley First School: Christmas Fair, Friday 27th November
articles.author: Gillian & Team FOSFS
articles.summary: Summer Fair raised £691.87; Santa’s grotto returns at the Christmas Fair, with a raffle and a call for helpers.
body: Grab a brew and catch up on what FOSFS has been up to since my last update… First of all, I want to start this month's article with a HUGE thank you to everyone who supported our Summer Fair! Drumroll please… we raised a fantastic £691.87! What an amazing total! We are absolutely delighted and so proud of what we achieved together.

A huge thank you to all our wonderful volunteers who turned up to help set up, run stalls and clear everything away afterwards. We really couldn't have done it without you. Thank you also to everyone who came along, spent their pennies and helped make the day such a success!

Next up is our Halloween Disco in October! The children absolutely love a disco, especially when they get to dress up, and it's always a brilliant event. We're looking forward to seeing some fantastic costumes!

Meanwhile, we're already working hard behind the scenes on our Christmas Fair on Friday 27th November. Please take a look at the poster for all the details and pop the date in your diary. And here's some exciting news… I've already spoken to Santa himself, and he's confirmed he'll be joining us in his wonderful grotto again this year! How lucky are we?!
As always, we'll need some extra pairs of hands to help set up and clear away. If you can spare even an hour, we'd love to hear from you. The kettle will be on, and the mince pies will be warmed!

We'll also be holding our Christmas raffle, and we'd be incredibly grateful for the support of our lovely local businesses. If you run a business and would like to donate a raffle prize, please get in touch with the school. Every donation, big or small, is very much appreciated. And if you'd like to buy some raffle tickets and be in with a chance of winning a lovely prize, please contact the school office.
It's the generosity and support of our wonderful village community that makes these events possible, and we really are grateful for every bit of help we receive.

Thank you, as always, for reading our article. If you'd like to support any of our events, please pop into the school office, give them a call on 01484 603230, or email: office@shepleyfirst.org Gillian & Team FOSFS

articles.author: Shepley Fields Forever
articles.summary: A proposed planning application off Penistone Road in Shelley, and the new national planning delegation scheme.
body: Recently we heard the not unexpected news that there is now a proposed planning application for fields off Penistone Road in Shelley. As a group we are now in contact with the new Shelley steering committee to offer any support and help we can.

The National Scheme of Delegation of Planning Functions is a way of scheduling how planning applications and objections may be dealt with in the future. This comes into force at the end of October. It is rather vague how it may affect our Shepley campaign, and others, and we hope for further information.
Of course, we will share any news and information we get. Until then, thank you for all your support and please keep the comments coming to: D.C.Admin@kirklees.gov.uk.

articles.title: Hear from our advertisers: ‘The Art Teacher’ – Catherine Johnson
articles.author: Catherine Johnson
articles.summary: Weekly adult art classes at St Paul’s Hall on Wednesday mornings, for all abilities – from a Holmfirth art teacher with 15 years’ experience.
body: Hello, my name is Catherine Johnson, aka ‘The Art Teacher’. I am embarking on a new teaching venture providing weekly adult Art classes and family Art sessions in the local community. I live in Holmfirth with my husband and two daughters. I have a BA and MA in Fine Art from The University of Leeds. Nowadays when I do get the chance to produce my own work, I really enjoy drawing and painting from natural themes. However, there is always something art and craft based on our kitchen table that the girls are creating!

I have 15 years’ experience teaching Art & Photography at GCSE and A Level in the local area. I enjoy teaching a wide range of artistic styles, materials and processes. I have been fortunate to work with countless fantastic young people. I have loved watching students’ confidence grow and celebrating their individual successes and achievements.

My first venture beyond the classroom was at ‘Art at the House’ at Cliffe House in September, where I had the opportunity to run drawing and painting workshops across the weekend. I thoroughly enjoyed creating fabulous artwork with people of all ages, as well as meeting and speaking with a whole host of lovely people. It was also great to catch up with numerous past students, many of which have their own families now!

My next venture is an adult class running at St. Paul’s Hall, Shepley, on a Wednesday 10am to 12pm. This class is for all abilities, from beginners to the more advanced. This is a sociable, relaxed class and definitely for anyone who thinks they ‘can’t draw but likes to have a go’. Everyone is welcome to come learn or hone an Art skill and create something fabulous, whilst having a cuppa and a nice chat.

The class runs during term-time and each week focuses upon a specific technique or process, with the aim to create a standalone piece each week. I demonstrate each technique and provide support throughout. All materials and refreshments are included. Over the weeks the class aim is to cover a wide range of materials and techniques; including drawing, painting, mixed media and some print making. I am also open to suggestions if there is a material or process people would like to try!
Classes are £18 per two hour session, all materials and refreshments included.
To book a taster class please email Catherine: theartteacherholmfirth@outlook.com
Take a look at my Facebook or Instagram pages ‘The Art Teacher Holmfirth’.
If this day and time does not suit, look out for new classes starting in the local area soon.

articles.title: Letter from our Member of Parliament: Working on issues raised by residents
articles.author: Jade Botterill MP
articles.summary: Penistone Road crossing repairs at Far Bank, power cuts and Northern Powergrid, and support for local micro-businesses.
body: October is an odd month. Summer is truly over, with the days shorter without the run-in to Christmas giving them purpose. I’ve been glad to see communities across our area still active with scarecrow festivals bringing people together.

With political parties having their conferences across the country, I’ve been able to spend more time at home focussed on local issues. I recently had a great meeting with local micro-businesses at Yummy Yorkshire to discuss what they need from me and the Government to help them thrive and grow. We spoke about our crackdown on late payments, which are holding back so many businesses: a great conversation in such a fantastic setting. I couldn’t resist the cakes!

In Shelley, I was delighted to confirm that the Penistone Road, at the bottom of Far Bank, will now be included in the council’s upcoming programme of repair works. This follows concerns from local residents raised with me at my recent coffee morning in the village hall. Highways have confirmed that the crossing is not operating correctly and the necessary works have been raised with their contractor. There isn’t a confirmed date just yet, but I’ll continue to chase for an update and make sure this progresses as quickly as possible.

I have also been working with local residents, Northern Powergrid, and GTC, to address recent, frequent power cuts that have had an unacceptable impact on people. Throughout my conversations with both organisations, I have been clear that the current level of service is not good enough; people should be able to cook dinner and watch TV without worrying about services cutting out and alarms going off. Since my meeting with them, Northern Powergrid believe they have identified the main fault, and begun communicating directly to customers, including through in-person community events. I want to thank their engineers, who have been working tirelessly to get this fixed, and am continuing to push for effective compensation for customers. I know the problems haven’t gone away fully, so please keep reaching out to me so I know where Northern Powergrid needs to be delivering more.

Since I became an MP, I’ve been able to really help hundreds of local people with issues ranging from passport delays and unfair fines, to getting the NHS care they deserve and their education. Helping people like this is one of the best parts of the job and also helps me launch wider campaigns to help our community. It was local people reaching out to me directly that gave me the full picture when getting answers from Northern Powergrid and when I bring up important policy issues in Parliament I always mention the stories of residents.
Contact: jade.botterill.mp@parliament.uk – if you have any issues I can support with, please reach out to me.

articles.title: Woodley School: Giants visit Woodley!
articles.author: Woodley School & College
articles.summary: Prize-winning giant vegetables from the Harrogate Autumn Flower Show inspire pupils’ horticulture skills.
body: ## Giants visit Woodley!
Earlier this month, Giant Vegetables from the Harrogate Autumn Flower Show visited Woodley School & College, a specialist school for pupils with autism in Huddersfield.

Paula Haley from the Professional Gardener's Guild (PGG) dropped in with prize winners grown by David Barker (PGG Vice Chairman) and other exhibitors to show the students the giants people have grown.

Paula said, "I had heard that Woodley wanted to develop their pupils' horticulture skills and thought what an amazing opportunity to show students what you can grow and to encourage excitement and enthusiasm. We need to do more to promote horticulture and this is a fabulous way to do it! It was enough excitement just to put them in my car and to bring them home!"

Mr Adrian Sugden (Headteacher) was delighted to accept such a "big surprise!" The staff at the school were equally amazed as the vegetables, including carrots, beetroot, marrows, leeks, onions, and pumpkins were wheeled up the path. Two of the individual vegetables weighed over 25kg.

The vegetables went on display for the day and were shown to all the school classes alongside examples from a local supermarket for comparison. Some of the children also had the opportunity to harvest the seeds from inside the vegetables.

Shepley resident, Miss Claire Thompson (Assistant Headteacher at Woodley), who also organised the surprise said, "How fantastic that David and the other exhibitors from Harrogate Flower Show wanted to support our students. We are very grateful and always welcome ideas like this from our local communities. We plan to use the seeds from these giants to grow our own next year! Careers information and experiences run throughout our curriculum, and this gave us a wonderful opportunity to talk about farming, horticulture and greengrocery as possible future careers for our pupils. Being hands on with the vegetables, touching and smelling them supports our pupils to develop their knowledge and understanding of the world around them."
If any local business would like to support Woodley School & College in enriching pupils' experiences with real-life work encounters or experiences, please do contact Claire at the school.

body: ## Looking after your wellbeing with the Kirklees Wellness Service

The Kirklees Wellness Service offers support to help local people make positive changes to their health and lifestyle. Whether you want to become more active, improve your diet, manage your weight, stop smoking or make other healthy lifestyle changes, the service can help you take that first step.

Improving your wellbeing doesn't have to mean changing everything at once. The Wellness Service can provide advice, encouragement and practical support to help you set realistic goals and build healthier habits.
If you're a Kirklees resident, find out more about the support available and see how the Kirklees Wellness Service could help you on your health and wellbeing journey.
Drop-in service: Shepley Library Mondays 3:00pm to 4:45pm or visit https://kirkleeswellnessservice.co.uk/ to find out more.
## The Mast Integrated Neighbourhood Teams
The Mast primary care network (PCN) comprises of five member GP surgeries Shepley, Kirkburton, Skelmanthorpe, Dearne Valley, Lepton and Kirkheaton. Together we serve over 35,000 registered patients.

Integrated Neighbourhood Teams (INTs) are multidisciplinary, collaborative groups bringing together health, social care, and voluntary sector professionals to deliver seamless, proactive, personalised care to local communities. They are a major government and NHS England initiative, designed to transform community health and care.

The INT acts as a single point of coordination to make sure patients with complex medical, social or rehabilitation needs can return home with the necessary care packages rather than staying unnecessarily in hospital or being discharged to a nursing home and reduces the likelihood of re-admission. Key benefits for the multidisciplinary team include a better understanding of what each team does, improved collaboration, better communication and reduced duplication of work.

The MAST INT was chosen as the first accelerator site in Kirklees, focusing on improving patient support after hospital discharge. Weekly meetings bring together multidisciplinary professionals from general practice, hospital, community, social care, mental health, and rehabilitation services to ensure all aspects of care are addressed.

articles.title: A snapshot of Shepley’s history: Lydgate Road
articles.author: Clare Francis
articles.summary: “Lidgit”: Joshua Wood’s shop and bakehouse, the 1879 fire, Lydgate House, Pinfold Cottage and the greengrocer’s pony and cart.
body: Pronounced as ‘Lidgit’ and even spelled as Lydgett, this road did originally have a gate on it. At the top of the road where it meets Station Road there are now modern houses, but there used to be some open land and a shop (right hand image). This combined grocers, confectioners and corn merchants was run by Joshua Wood and later after Joshua’s death by his son Frank. Adjoining the shop were one or two cottages and Joshua also had his own bakehouse. In December 1879 there was a small fire in the shop. An overheating chimney flue set fire to nearby cloth goods. Joshua, together with Police Constable Ingham managed to get the burning goods outside and doused the flames with buckets of water, but £100 of stock was destroyed. Fortunately, the shop had insurance.

Further down the road was Lydgate House, another laith house (that combined accommodation for both the family and their animals), although this property had weaver’s windows on its upper floors. This house was later occupied by Walter Wortley, a merchant tailor.
Pinfold Cottage was so named because it was sited near the pinfold, a place where stray animals were penned up. The gate may well have been part of this structure.
At 4 Lydgate until about the 1950s there was a greengrocer called George Henry Heeley who used to go round the village selling greengrocery with a pony and shandy (horse and cart).
Dyke Bottom was also marked on maps although its name too has had numerous spellings over the years.
— Clare Francis
With thanks to Norman Smith and David Billington’s team (who completed and shared much of this thorough research).

articles.title: Shepley Bird and Wildlife Group: A love for the wild & our duty to protect it
articles.author: Cathy Evans
articles.summary: PC Caroline Newsome on wildlife crime, a badger stuck on a roof, and next month’s ‘Tales From a River Bank’.
body: Our October talk was given by PC Caroline Newsome – Kirklees Wildlife, Rural and Heritage Crime Officer, Badger Crime Tactical Delivery Group. Caroline was accompanied by two representatives of the badger groups in Huddersfield and various examples of wildlife of the area (taxidermied!).

Caroline began the talk by giving us some details about her background in the police where she has been in a variety of roles, and in her passion for wildlife and nature. Currently she has pets, chickens, fosters hedgehogs for Shelley Hedgehog group, and keeps eight disabled hedgehogs safe in her garden.
It was made clear how difficult it is to investigate wildlife crime – there are rarely witnesses or CCTV evidence etc and of course the animals and birds cannot tell us their stories.

We were given a list of the sorts of crimes and incidents that are investigated – and each one led on to a story about an example of these crimes. Some were very distressing to hear, but Caroline’s passion for her job and her stories of other kinds of incidents gave us relief from the difficulty of witnessing the cruelty that some people show.

One of the most endearing incidents was of a badger – stuck on a roof! The house involved was on a steep hill, where the garden above was on a level with the roof concerned. The badger had clearly wandered off, fallen down a level onto the roof and was unable to get back up. Caroline and colleagues Sue, Rob and Fletch made a two-pronged rescue attempt – Caroline herself on a ladder at the front of the house trying to attract the badger’s attention with Sue holding her steady and Fletch and Rob up on the roof attempting and ultimately succeeding to get the very alarmed badger into a cage. Fortunately, the animal was rescued and released but unfortunately, the rest of that day was spent with one rescuer receiving treatment at A & E for a severe badger bite to the hand!

There are a number of local organisations – like Shelley Hedgehogs and the Badger groups – that help out with the work that Caroline does and she acknowledged that she would find it extremely difficult to do her work without them.

As always, the talk was greeted with a round of applause – with an extra appreciation for the difficulty of Caroline’s work, and how glad we are that she is there to do it! Cathy Evans Our next indoor meeting is on Wednesday 4th November at 7.30pm, Cliffe House, Coach House when Mick Forster Jones from The River Holme Connections Group will be giving us ‘Tales From a River Bank’. This is a great chance to learn more about the area in which we live.
— Cathy Evans

articles.title: Cliffe House: A celebration of creativity and community
articles.author: Nigel Hoyle & the Art at the House team
articles.summary: Art at the House welcomed over 2,000 visitors, a new stone monolith sculpture and a real piano in the woods.
body: Dear Community,

We are always really excited as Art at the House approaches and this year it took place at Cliffe House on Saturday 19th and Sunday 20th September. This time the feeling was a little different. With an expanded committee of five volunteers and with support from the outstanding Cliffe House staff we had much more to look forward to.

With generous funding from Kirklees Seasons of Culture and Kirkburton Parish Council, along with sponsorship from several local businesses, we were able to expand onto the front lawn at Cliffe House and grow the woodland market into something really special. A stone monolith sculpture was permanently put in place by sculptor Ryan James and will be finished with your help over the next couple of years at the event. We finally managed to get a real piano into the woods which sounded magical! We introduced some new dimensions to the event but essentially, this was a celebration of creativity and community engagement. The feedback we have had from stall holders and the public has been overwhelmingly positive though we have learned some lessons which will help us to improve our planning for next year.

Aside from a bit of rain on the Saturday morning the weather was kind and for the most part the sun came out and brought great vibes with it. We counted well over 2000 people at the gates over the weekend who came and took part in lots of workshops, listened to live music and bought quality art and crafts.
Art At The House is a not-for-profit Community Interest Company and this year for the first time we asked for your donations to help us grow the event and you did not disappoint, thank you!

As for this year’s event we would like to say a huge THANK YOU to you the Shepley community for supporting the event through thick and thin. We live in a very special village. https://artatthehouse.co.uk/ Follow us @artatthehouse Nigel Hoyle and the ArtattheHouse Team

The poppies were introduced for the Heritage Day a couple of weeks ago, reflecting the effort put into the event.

body: We’re delighted to announce that Shepley Cricket Club will once again host its annual Bonfire & Firework Display on Thursday 5th November. This much-loved event has grown in popularity year on year, drawing crowds from across the local area as well as our own village community.
## Ticketing success

A particular highlight in 2025 was the move to electronic ticketing. To be honest, it exceeded expectations, making life much easier for our volunteers, speeding things up for spectators arriving at the ground, and was very well received by everyone who used it. Suffice to say we are continuing with this initiative, and we ask you to scan the QR code to purchase your tickets then bring them along on the day (even add to your Apple Wallet!)
## Parking & access

Despite asking for support from the local authorities and the police regarding Marsh Lane and surrounding roads, this has never gained any traction. What has been made very clear is that Shepley Cricket Club is not permitted to make any attempts to manage or control traffic or parking on the public highway.

We kindly ask all Shepley residents to walk to the club if possible. If you must drive, please be considerate of those living nearby — and park as you would hope others would, if the event was happening outside your own home.
We look forward to welcoming you for another fantastic evening.

articles.title: Shepley Cricket Club: Bringing the season to a close
articles.author: Matthew Hartley, Chairman
articles.summary: Senior Presentation Night awards, the league-winning Under-9s and work starting on the Nursery Ground.
body: Our Senior Presentation Night brought the curtain down on another season at Shepley Cricket Club and gave us the opportunity to celebrate the achievements, commitment and community spirit that make our club so special.

It is always one of my favourite evenings of the year. Whilst many of the trophies recognise performances on the field, it is also a chance to thank the many people whose contribution often goes unseen. Whether you've spent your summer playing, scoring, coaching, fundraising, preparing teas, serving behind the bar, maintaining the ground, or simply cheering the teams on from the boundary, you've helped make 2026 another memorable year for the club.

It was particularly pleasing to see individual contributions recognised through awards such as the Trevor Curtis Trophy (Alison Rose) and Junior Clubman of the Year (Kitty Dawson), alongside the achievements of our senior and junior teams. It was also wonderful to celebrate our Huddersfield League-winning Under- 9s alongside the senior players. Seeing our youngest cricketers sharing the stage with our senior teams was a timely reminder that the future of the club is in good hands.

Renovation work on the square is underway, with essential repairs and maintenance taking place to ensure it is in the best possible condition for the 2027 season. Also, anyone who has walked past the club recently will have noticed work beginning on our Nursery Ground, a project that has been the focus of so much fundraising and planning throughout 2026. Seeing diggers on site makes all those sleepless nights, fundraising events and grant applications feel worthwhile, although there is still plenty of work ahead before the project is complete.

Whilst the club is seldom used during winter, this perhaps makes it even more important that we are keeping an eye on the little things. Keeping the building up to temperature, watching out for those little bits of damp that can, over a short period of time, turn a small issue into a big problem, and generally making sure everything is ready for when cricket returns next spring.
Before we know it, thoughts will turn to winter nets and another cricket season. Until then, winter well, and we look forward to welcoming everyone back to Shepley Cricket Club in 2027.
— Matthew Hartley, Chairman, Shepley Cricket Club

articles.title: Welcome to September’s edition
articles.author: Shepley Magazine Team
articles.summary: Volunteering opportunities across the village, Art at the House, and the Shepley Over The Years exhibition.
body: Here in Shepley, we are very lucky to have so many people volunteering to make life better for our local residents. We’ve mentioned it before, but it really is a life affirming thing to give up your free time to improve the lives of other people. Perhaps if you’re retired and feeling at a bit of a loose end, volunteering could be just the thing to lift your spirits whilst also supporting the village. In this issue you’ll find several opportunities to join groups as a volunteer.

Please have a look through the various articles and see if you would like to get involved. Even this magazine is looking for extra people to help with deliveries, so you could help the community whilst getting fit at the same time!

There are a couple of local events this month that are heavily reliant on volunteers. One is Art at the House at Cliffe House on Saturday 19th and Sunday 20th. This is a hugely popular free event with something for all the family. You’ll find entertainment, food, a woodland market, various displays and of course the chance to admire and buy original pieces of artwork. Have a look at the poster in this month’s issue for full details. There are no admission charges and parking is available, but if you live in the village, walking is the best option.

Another free village event is the Shepley Over The Years exhibition at St Paul’s Church Hall on Saturday 12th and Sunday 13th, from 2pm. This is part of Heritage Open Days which is a nationwide event run every September to celebrate England’s heritage and culture. It’s run by volunteers and full details can be found on their website: https://www.heritageopendays.org.uk/about-us/press.html Raising money for charity is another positive option for benefitting society. We are very lucky, in this country, to have so many people who will give up their time freely to help charities. In this month’s issue we have the final instalment of local man, Shaun Casey’s run from John o’ Groats to Land’s End raising money for Marie Curie and in the letters page news of another local man, Dave Chew, who is raising money for The Alzheimer’s Society. Very well done to them both.

articles.title: Shaun Casey: From Carlisle to Land’s End
articles.author: Shaun Casey
articles.summary: The second half of a 48-day run from John o’ Groats to Land’s End, raising £12,410 for Marie Curie.
body: When I left Carlisle and wrote the last article, I still had a long way to go. The first part of the journey had taken us from John o’ Groats through some of the most remote and spectacular parts of Scotland, but from Carlisle onwards the landscape, the challenges and the weather changed considerably. I was also now on my own, as Grant had gone home to recover from his injury.

From Carlisle I headed south along the Cumbrian Way through the Lake District to Coniston Water, then on to Preston, Southport and Liverpool before crossing into Wales. I followed Offa’s Dyke through Wales before crossing the Severn Bridge and eventually joining the South West Coast Path. I then made my way through Somerset, Devon and Cornwall.

There were many fantastic days, and there were also some days when my feet hurt and the miles seemed to go on forever. But the people I met along the way continued to be incredibly generous, kind and supportive. They bought me drinks and meals, let me camp in their gardens and stopped in their droves to have a chat and ask what I was doing.

Donations continued to come in from complete strangers I met along the way, friends back home and people who had found my blog and simply wanted to support me. Every donation, whether from someone I knew or someone I had only just met, gave me a real lift and helped make the challenge feel like something bigger than just me running from one end of the country to the other.

A huge thank you to everyone who sponsored me, supported me, followed the journey or simply stopped for a chat. And a special thank you to those in Shepley who donated to the challenge. Your support was very much appreciated.

To get from John o’ Groats to Land’s End, in 48 days, I took more than 2.3 million steps, ran (and walked) a total of 1,192 miles, climbed the equivalent of 4.5 times the height of Everest and raised £12,410 including Gift Aid.
Grant also completed the challenge. When he recovered two weeks later, he went back to Carlisle with his bike and rode down to Land’s End, completing his journey a week before I finished mine.
So, we did what we set out to do, and both did Britain End to End. If you would like to contribute to Marie Curie, the link is: justgiving.com/page/britainendtoend Shaun Casey

articles.title: The W.H. Senior MBE Yorkshire Studies Group: The origins of the group
articles.author: Yorkshire Studies Group
articles.summary: How Mr W. H. Senior’s local history classes became today’s group; autumn term starts 1st October.
body: I first came across Mr Senior of Denby Dale in the mid 1960s when he taught an evening class held in Shepley First School. In those days there were many classes and interest groups to choose from meeting in various venues in local villages.

Mr Senior’s subject was ‘Local History’. He was so enthusiastic, interesting and inspiring that his classes were soon oversubscribed. He also led many trips to local historical buildings and churches where he would point out things of special interest. We occasionally went as far as the Yorkshire Dales.

Many years later when I retired, I discovered he was still passing on his knowledge at meetings in Shepley Methodist Church. He had established the ‘Yorkshire Studies Group’ in 1997: “To promote interest in the history and heritage of our district and the great county of Yorkshire”. Robert Carter of Kirkburton supported him in his talks and accompanied Mr Senior to Buckingham Palace to receive his MBE award for his unwavering services to local history.

When Mr Senior died at the age of 95 in 2000, Robert Carter continued to run the group until his own health failed. Since there was much enthusiasm for the group to continue it was taken on by Pauline Taylor and Dinah Bentley from 2014 to 2025. There is still plenty of interest in the group which is now run by Edward Willis, Martin Whitbread and Lesley Furniss.
The first meeting for the autumn term will be 1st October at 2.00pm at Shepley Methodist Church. New and established members will be very welcome and you may pay on the door. Angela Tolson

articles.title: Shepley Women’s Institute: Our groups continued over the summer
articles.author: Shepley WI
articles.summary: Neal’s Yard Remedies, the Striders and Strollers, the Gardening Group and Book Club.
body: Our July members’ meeting saw us sampling the products brought in by Neal’s Yard Remedies representative Tee, who provided lots of information about the benefits of herbal and aromatherapy products. We had good fun doing the ‘sniff tests’ to see if we could distinguish, for example, geranium from rosemary and other scents. We were all surprised at the pleasant scent of patchouli - very different from how most of us remembered it from the 1970s!

Both walking groups enjoyed lovely sunshine at their last outings. Our Striders, accompanied by Enzo the dog, explored the moors above Hade Edge, with views across Winscar, Harden and Snailsden reservoirs. Afterwards we had coffee at Totties Garden Centre at Scholes (once we had navigated the closed roads and diversion!)
Meanwhile, our Strollers explored the nooks and crannies of Shepley village, followed by a delicious and excellent value for money lunch at Paula’s Community Café in St Paul’s Hall.
Also outdoors, the Gardening Group has been busy helping to clear the border outside Shepley Library, as well as sharing their successes and failures in this summer’s drought.

The Crafts and Crumbs group continues to meet on the fourth Monday of the month, alongside the café regulars at Shepley Methodist Church. Recently, members have been focusing on their own projects, but no doubt, as we move into autumn (and, dare I say it, edge ever closer to Christmas!), we’ll be experimenting with ideas for seasonal gifts and decorations.
Book Club members also met during the summer break to share their holiday reading.
Our next members’ meeting is at 7:30pm on Wednesday 16th September, when our speaker will be Paul Jefferies on the subject of ‘Sustainable Tea and Coffee’. Debra

articles.title: Shepley Naturalists’ Society: Still hot; still dry
articles.author: Shepley Naturalists’ Society
articles.summary: A stroll around Royd Moor Reservoir and the Silkstone walk and lunch.
body: ## Royd Moor Reservoir

Nine naturalists enjoyed a delightful 2½ mile stroll around Royd Moor Reservoir. The hedgerows and meadows were bursting with wildflowers, including Common Milk Peas, Vetches, Pink Campions, Sneezeworts and delicate Harebells. Wildlife was abundant: a graceful heron stood quietly by the water's edge while mallards with their ducklings paddled by.

Swallows swooped low across the water to feed. Butterflies were no strangers, Cabbage Whites, Peacocks and Gatekeepers were seen fluttering among the bankside flowers. Margaret Lucas Digley-Holme round The walk around Digley Reservoir was on a late July day. It is popular with people and a favourite of ours too. Not one of the hottest days but warm enough to make rucksacks feel heavy and clothes excessive. The heat was perhaps the cause of an absence of birds; Digley Reservoir has never attracted more than a few species of waterbirds, although a family of dabchicks and mallards had been busy a few days before our visit. As for waders, although Curlew are often heard nearby and tiny Common Sandpiper regularly feed along the shore, it is the striking groups of Oyster-Catchers that gather and breed along the embankment; and the woods are usually alive with birdsong, but not today. A large hairy caterpillar, perhaps a "woolly bear", crossed our path leading to tales of sightings of real bears, but sadly nowhere in West Yorkshire. Yellow Rattle was still out in abundance, more brown now than yellow, but still clear evidence of fields that have been traditionally managed. Coming back down through the hayfields, known in earlier times as the Shays, towards the embankment, we spotted two pairs of ears in the field below us - hares in their forms? Or rabbits perhaps? As we swapped opinions they suddenly stood to their full height and raced off down towards the wall, reappearing at the gateway leading to the ever-present herd of highland cattle. Hares, then! Back to the cars finally seeing an oystercatcher rising up loudly from the embankment; we also saw swooping martins and swallows, then the rare sight of a large group of lapwings splashing and preening on the stony edge in preparation for their coming flight away from their breeding grounds; and over them all a buzzard floating languidly above.
— Pauline Taylor and David Fisher
## Silkstone walk and lunch

These occasional but regular walks culminating in a pub meal always manage to attract a considerable number of members. Sue has found a winning formula where half of us opt to walk and the other half head straight for the pub! Rodger led us through the attractive and historic village of Silkstone, pausing to read the poignant account of the Huskar Pit disaster of 1838 carved on a substantial monument in the churchyard. Twenty- six children aged between 7 and 17 were drowned in the flooded mine. Reaching the track bed of the former wagonway we followed it through the woods and ambled back up to the Bells (formerly Ring o' Bells) where we were welcomed with an excellent meal and cooling drinks. David Fisher Contact: Sue Whitehouse 605614 or David Fisher 682903 or website: shepley-naturalists.weebly.com

articles.title: Shepley Bird and Wildlife Group: That friendly Robin may be Russian!
articles.author: Shepley Bird and Wildlife Group
articles.summary: Winter visitors to look out for, and indoor meetings restarting on 2nd September.
body: Did you know that our resident population of Robins, that traditional bird of the Christmas card, will be joined by Robins from Europe, Scandinavia and Russia, all finding our climate easier to endure before flying back home in the spring?

If you’re looking forward to the cooler days ahead, then we have some wonderful suggestions for warm and entertaining evenings close to home in Cliffe House with our new programme of talks. All these are designed to be of interest to beginners and the more experienced and our speakers are happy to answer any and all questions.

By venturing outside with us on our field visits, we hope to increase your love and understanding of birds and wildlife. Discover how any winter blues can be blown away in an instant with sightings of migrant birds arriving to enjoy our warmer winter climate and sharing that experience with others.

Our indoor meetings start on Wednesday September 2nd at 7.30pm, Cliffe House, Coach House when Ray Brown the local wildlife photographer will be telling us more about his favourite studies of birds and animals. To attend as a visitor there is a charge of £3.00.

Field visits are free so just let us know if you’d like to join us and we can promise fresh air and a great deal of good humour. Feel free to pick and mix any of the talks or field visits or join the group for the modest fee of £15 per year.
Details of all our talks will be available in these monthly magazine articles and programmes from your local libraries or by request using the contact details below. We look forward to welcoming you.

articles.title: Shepley Methodist Church: A fun celebration of Yorkshire Day
articles.author: Revd Sue Pegg
articles.summary: Yorkshire dialect readings, Fat Rascals and Yorkshire tea – plus Harvest and Remembrance services coming up.
body: YORKSHIRE DAY (officially August 1st) came into being initially in 1975 as a protest against some in local government who were wanting to mess with the county's boundaries. It seemed that their protest was successful and from then on Yorkshire Day has been celebrated around the county in lots of places with the events taking many different forms.
Shepley Methodist Church decided to have a fun celebration of Yorkshire Day this year on the nearest Sunday which was August 2nd and everyone was invited.

The church was decorated with the white rose of Yorkshire flag and bunting and even a few balloons with a sheep logo on them and the celebration comprised of poems, a light-hearted quiz and songs, and even our bible reading (taken from the Yorkshire Passport!) was spoken in the Yorkshire dialect.

The children coloured in a picture of a Yorkshire man with his flat cap and completed a wordsearch too. Highlights were the ‘Ode to the Emley Tower’ written and presented by Maggie (see last month's magazine) and Rita singing ‘Scarborough Fair’.

There was lots of laughter, and we even recalled the founder of Methodism, John Wesley’s experience in the county when he wrote in his diary, "I rode over the mountains to Huddersfield. A wilder people I never saw in England. The men, women and children filled the streets as we rode along and seemed ready to devour us" and then when visiting nearby Barnsley, he said, "I turned aside to Barnsley famous for all manner of wickedness," so not such a good write up from Mr Wesley.

We did acknowledge the painful times endured by many in our county during and for many years after the Industrial Revolution when workers flocked to the towns in search of work and lived in appalling conditions. This was summed up in the Dalesman’s Litany.
Our celebration continued afterwards when there were buns made to the famous Fat Rascal recipe, Yorkshire ginger cake and buttered scones for everyone, all washed down with a cup of Yorkshire tea.
It was good fun and a great joy to celebrate our County of Yorkshire as a part of God's creation.

We have two celebrations coming up soon at Shepley Methodist Church. The first is our HARVEST FESTIVAL on Sunday 11th October led by Church Minister, Revd Sue and then secondly our CHURCH ANNIVERSARY on 25th October, led by preacher Kimm Brooke.

There is also a service for REMEMBRANCE SUNDAY, 8th November, led by Revd Sue, you might like to pop into your diary. Everyone is welcome to all the services and of course any Sunday morning at Shepley Methodist Church when we start at 10.45am. It would be lovely to see you.
Contact: Revd Sue Pegg – 07931 832456

articles.title: A snapshot of Shepley’s history: Yew Tree Road
articles.author: Clare Francis
articles.summary: A 1685 farmhouse, rows of weavers’ cottages, a market garden and the cattle dealers of Yew Tree Road.
body: Yew Tree Road is marked on the early maps of Shepley and literally led to woodland rich in yew trees. Linking Station Road to the old toll road (Abbey Road) it has a brook flowing through the bottom which is still visible at some points. In 1859 a tenant farmer was prosecuted because chemicals from his dye house had killed all the fish downstream.

At the top of the hill near Station Road is a farmhouse built in 1685 by Edward Walker. His initials are still over the door. Originally a laith house, where the occupants lived on one side and the animals on the other, the property has since been divided into two homes.

Most of the houses actually bordering the road are fairly modern, but there are older rows of cottages, commonly known as the Co-op rows as they were built by the Shepley Co-operative Society. The top row was constructed in the 1920s and the bottom row in the 1930s.

As the road rises towards the main road there was once a market garden containing numerous greenhouses called Rillside. This was run by Albert Kaye. He had a wooden greengrocer’s shop nearby, where he sold his produce. He would often be working in the garden so if customers called, they used a bell to summon him. The shop tended to get busy at weekends and Roger Smith remembered watching the queues from his home as a boy, then dashing across the field to make his purchases when it got quieter.
Other residents included George and Turner Woodhead and Willie Payne, all cattle dealers.
— Clare Francis
With thanks to Norman Smith and David Billington’s team (who completed and shared much of this thorough research).

articles.title: Central Co-op: New Mill Community Fun Day
articles.author: Central Co-op
articles.summary: A summer fun day for families with stalls, educational activities and a free picnic.
body: We had a lovely day at the invitation of OurCoop to attend the New Mill Community Fun Day.

This is a yearly event where OurCoop brings families together over the summer holidays. The Membership & Community Council who fund the day provide co-operative education activities to highlight the recreational and educational activities that the Society provides.

A number of stall holders attended from Kirklees Council. Riverholme provided educational work from bug houses to identifying different water species in the garden. A Scrap Plastic workshop was offered and other activities included weaving of willow fishes, potato printing and stone painting. The volunteers at the Community Garden also provided the opportunity for the young people to do some potting and learning about the gardens and showcasing this wonderful oasis of beautiful gardens and woodland which was a pleasure for everyone.

The event concluded with a free picnic provided by OurCoop with sandwiches, crisps, drinks and cake, which is always a highlight when the food arrives. People then take their time to sit around in the surroundings to enjoy time together as a family. This year over 170 people attended and each year it seems to grow and opening the gardens to so many people was a joy. Tanya Noon

articles.title: Letter from our Member of Parliament: New planning rules – vape and gaming shops
articles.author: Jade Botterill MP
articles.summary: New powers for councils over vape and betting shops, SCARD, and opening Shelley Gala.
body: Cllr Richard Smith: richard.smith@kirklees.gov.uk Tel: 07799 310725 or Cllr Bill Armer: bill.armer@kirklees.gov.uk Tel: 07954578077 Parliament breaks for recess over summer, meaning I get to spend more time in our area. Now I’ve made no secret that I prefer spending time out in our community to being in Westminster (nothing beats a good Yorkshire welcome or a day at a gala!), but it also provides a real chance to have important conversations with people across our towns and villages.

One thing that has come up recently has been concerns about increased numbers of vape and betting shops in nearby towns, making their high streets less appealing as they crowd out the shops and services people love and rely on. I’ve spoken often with my colleagues about the need to tackle this issue and I am proud that the Government is putting power back in the hands of local communities to have a real say over what opens on their high street. We are putting in place new planning rules to ensure vape shops and adult gaming centres can’t just pop up without local people having a say and to give councils the power to ban them near schools. I will work with Kirklees Council to make sure they use these powers to rebuild pride in towns near us.

I also met with SCARD, an amazing local organisation that supports families who have lost loved ones in road traffic accidents. They provide 1-1 support and counselling for as long as the person needs it, being there when people need it most. SCARD is run by people with such compassion and care, and I am proud to support them in their work.

I also had the real privilege to open Shelley Gala at the Cricket Club. It’s such an amazing event, bringing together our community for over 90 years! Events like this can only happen with the hard work of volunteers. With help all the way from Shelley's Over 60s Club down to the children at Shelley First School, it was a real testament to the entire community, and I was so happy to be there.
The work the Government and I are doing originates from conversations I’ve had with local people, so as ever, do reach out to me and my team.
Contact: jade.botterill.mp@parliament.uk – if you have any issues I can support with, please reach out to me.

articles.title: Shepley Health Centre: Five things patients can do
articles.author: Shepley Health Centre
articles.summary: Flu clinic dates and World Patient Safety Day: five things patients can do.
body: ## Flu season 2026 – save the date

Appointments are now available for our forthcoming flu campaign. Our main clinic will be on: Saturday 3rd October 2026 at Shepley Health Centre. Other dates are also available. We have enough vaccinations for all eligible patients.
## World Patient Safety Day 17th September 2026

World Patient Safety Day reminds us that safer healthcare is a shared responsibility. In 2026, the focus is on making care safer for people living with long-term conditions such as diabetes, heart disease, cancer and chronic respiratory diseases.
## 5 things patients can do
- 1. Ask questions If you are unsure about your diagnosis, treatment or care plan, ask your healthcare team to explain.
- 2. Know your medicines Keep an up-to-date list of your medicines and understand what each one is for and how to take it.
- 3. Check your information Make sure important details—such as your name, medicines, allergies and medical history—are correct.
- 4. Understand what happens next Before leaving an appointment or hospital, make sure you know what follow-up care, tests or appointments are needed.
- 5. Speak up If something doesn't seem right or you are worried about your care, tell a member of your healthcare team. Your concerns matter.

articles.author: Readers
articles.summary: Thanks to a local optician, and to the Friends of Cliffe House.
body: Dear Shepley Magazine, I have a quite complex eye disease that has required surgery and constant ongoing treatment and this has meant at least three return visits a year to the Leeds General Infirmary eye clinic.

I am of course hugely grateful to the NHS for the expert care and treatment that I have received. However, the many routine visits to Leeds and the long waits in crowded corridors have been less than welcome, so I was really delighted to discover that the Kirburton Eye Care Practice could offer me the same remedial treatment. The advantages are of course obvious in that they are so close to Shepley and additionally, will always fit me in quickly if I am experiencing any discomfort.

I have found the opticians here wonderfully caring and supportive and also qualified to deliver far more services than you might at first think and it is these extra services that have made such a difference to how my ongoing eye care is managed.
I cannot recommend this practice highly enough; we are so fortunate to have them so near to where we live. Chris Marks Thank you for your support.

Thank you to the Friends of Cliffe House for providing the opportunity at Cliffe House Summer Fair for me to have a charity fundraising table in aid of the Alzheimer’s Society. We were selling home-made biscuits and children’s books, and I am pleased to say we raised £244.50. You can still give to the Alzheimer’s Society at https://www.justgiving.com/page/david-chew-4 Thank you, Dave Chew Dear Readers, can I invite you to Art At The House 2026 Saturday 19th & Sunday 20th September 10am – 4pm Meet - our 60+ amazing artists Try - some of our 23 workshops or other activities Buy – High quality Art and Craft work that cannot be found on the high street Enjoy – live music and performance throughout the weekend FREE ENTRY Local History Group display at the Heritage event Hi... don't forget to bring your memories of life in Shepley and to leave them and/or your contact details with The Local History Group display at the Heritage event in St Paul's 11th and 12th September. articles.title: Shepley Bowling Club: Hot stuff on the Green
articles.author: Shepley Bowling Club
articles.summary: A scorching season on the green, the Drawn Pairs and the Men’s Singles.
body: Wow, what an amazing, but very unusual bowling season we are experiencing. Never has it been known before for the ladies to have to rearrange or cancel matches due to the heat, at the advice of the League.
Trying to keep the bowls on the Green has been a challenge, games taking much longer, as we collect the woods that have ended up in the ‘ditch’. Good fun, tricky and very different.

We held the DRAWN PAIRS on Friday 7th August, our most popular event, so well attended and enjoyed by all, again helped by the beautiful balmy evening it was. Thank you to everyone who supported this event, there was some super bowling. Congratulations to the four well-deserved finalists, Liz Hirst and Andrew Astbury, our winners, beating Laura Bateman and John Pearman in an exciting final.

The MEN’S SINGLES was played on Tuesday 11th August, again the weather helped to make it a success. There was some superb bowling, considering the condition of the Green due to the extremely hot weather. Grant Richardson and Andrew Astbury played a brilliant final game, Grant being the worthy winner.

articles.title: Shepley Cricket Club: Spotlight on Women’s and Girls’ cricket
articles.author: Shepley Cricket Club
articles.summary: A fundraising drive for a new artificial pitch, and a breakthrough season for women’s and girls’ cricket.
body: ## Around the club

As summer begins to wind down, so too does another busy cricket season at Shepley. It takes a huge effort from our volunteers and ground staff to keep pace with the constant activity — especially during the peak weeks when cup fixtures stack on top of already full league schedules. That effort continues to be one of our greatest strengths, and we remain incredibly proud of the amount of cricket we are able to facilitate at Marsh Lane.

This month we are shining a spotlight on the fantastic progress made across our Women’s and Girls’ sections. With a few fixtures still to come for the Senior Men’s and the odd junior game, a full round up of the season for those teams follows in the next edition.
## Fundraising

Back in May, we set an ambitious fundraising target of £31,000 to support the development of a new all-weather nursery ground. This project will allow us to expand opportunities for Women’s, Girls’ and Junior cricket, easing pressure on our main square which is already stretched to capacity. Thanks to the generosity of the local community — and a significant contribution from Sport England (The National Lottery) — we are well on our way to making this vision a reality.
Once the season ends, we hope to quickly see the ground being developed in the hope that the new pitch will be up and running for the 2027 season!
## Women’s cricket

After entering just one softball team in 2025, we took a huge step forward this year with one hardball team and two softball teams competing in 2026. That leap has transformed our programme: the number of games played has risen dramatically, and with league standings at stake, the cricket has been far more competitive.
In our first ever season of Women’s Hardball Cricket, the team currently sits 2nd in the league.
Although our fixtures are complete, a couple of other results could see us finish 3rd — but either way, ending the season in the top three is an outstanding achievement.

Our Women’s 1st Softball team enjoyed a perfect campaign, finishing top of the league with eight wins from eight. The Women’s 2nd Softball team also impressed, finishing 2nd, winning seven of their nine matches.

Across the summer, our women’s teams played 30 games, with 24 women representing the club — a breakthrough season in every sense. A huge well done to all players, organisers, coaches and umpires who made it possible.
## Girls’ cricket
This year we entered teams into both the U11 and U13 Girls’ leagues.
The U13 Girls spent most of the season near the top of the table, narrowly missing out on the title after a close defeat to Thongsbridge CC in the penultimate game.
Their batting and bowling were consistently excellent, but it was the teams fielding and teamwork that truly stood out — something regularly praised by opposition coaches as well as our own.

For the U11 Girls, the focus is on festival-style cricket with round-robin formats. Results matter far less at this age; it’s all about participation, enjoyment and learning the game. The girls embraced every opportunity brilliantly.

Any girls in the village who want to get involved please let us know. The number of girls participating at cricket, either girls only or mixed, has increased massively in recent years. We now offer cricket for girls from aged 5 through to senior women’s cricket and everything in between – softball, and a little bit of hardball if you are feeling brave!
Until next month…when hopefully I can summarise the season for all the other teams, maybe even some good news with the 2nd Team currently sitting top of the league…fingers crossed.
